3. Recapping Greedy Decoding
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446293141-172264885.png
This connects back to greedy decoding, already covered generally in Sampling. Greedy decoding genuinely commits to the single best word at every step, never reconsidering.

A genuinely early good-looking choice can genuinely lead to a genuinely worse overall sequence later on, a genuinely real limitation that beam search, explored throughout the rest of this topic, directly addresses.
4. Tracking Multiple Beams
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446293336-815514371.png
This connects back to recapping greedy decoding, already covered in this topic. Beam search genuinely tracks several partial sequences, called beams, in parallel instead of just one.
Each genuinely beam represents one genuinely different candidate continuation being explored at once, the exact core mechanism explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 5. Expanding And Pruning Beams
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446293337-636923119.png
This connects back to tracking multiple beams, already covered in this topic. At every genuinely step, each beam genuinely expands with several possible next words.

Only the genuinely top-scoring beams overall genuinely survive into the next step; the rest genuinely get pruned away, a genuinely repeated expand-and-prune cycle explored throughout the rest of this topic.
6. Sequence Scoring With Log Probabilities
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446293338-328689475.png
This connects back to expanding and pruning beams, already covered in this topic. Each genuinely beam's own overall score is genuinely the sum of log probabilities across all its tokens.
Log probabilities are genuinely used instead of raw probabilities to avoid extremely tiny numbers, a genuinely practical numerical detail explored throughout the rest of this topic.

https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446293338-877736460.png

This connects back to sequence scoring with log probabilities, already covered in this topic. A genuinely wider beam explores genuinely more candidate sequences, often finding a genuinely better overall result.
A genuinely wider beam also genuinely costs proportionally more compute at every single step, a genuinely real, tunable tradeoff explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 8. Beam Search Versus Sampling
This connects back to beam width tradeoff, already covered in this topic. Beam search genuinely searches for the single most likely overall sequence, with genuinely no randomness at all.

Random sampling, already covered generally in Sampling, genuinely embraces randomness for genuinely varied, creative output instead, a genuinely fundamental difference explored throughout the rest of this topic.

10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates a small beam search, already covered in this topic, tracking and pruning candidate sequences over two steps.

code.content:
import math

# already covered as the probability distribution over the vocabulary in Sampling
step_1_probs = {"the": 0.5, "a": 0.3, "this": 0.2}
step_2_probs_given_the = {"cat": 0.4, "dog": 0.35, "fox": 0.25}
step_2_probs_given_a = {"cat": 0.3, "dog": 0.3, "fox": 0.4}

def log_prob(p):
    return math.log(p)

# already covered as tracking multiple beams in this topic
beam_width = 2
step_1_candidates = [([word], log_prob(p)) for word, p in step_1_probs.items()]
step_1_candidates.sort(key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
beams = step_1_candidates[:beam_width]  # already covered as expanding and pruning beams in this topic

print(f"Step 1 beams (already covered in this topic): {beams}")

step_2_candidates = []
for sequence, score in beams:
    next_probs = step_2_probs_given_the if sequence[-1] == "the" else step_2_probs_given_a
    for word, p in next_probs.items():
        # already covered as sequence scoring with log probabilities in this topic
        new_sequence = sequence + [word]
        new_score = score + log_prob(p)
        step_2_candidates.append((new_sequence, new_score))

step_2_candidates.sort(key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
final_beams = step_2_candidates[:beam_width]

print(f"\nStep 2 beams after expanding and pruning (already covered in this topic): {final_beams}")

blocks.content: Running this example shows only the top-scoring sequences surviving from step to step, exactly the expand-and-prune cycle already covered in this topic, discarding lower-scoring beams along the way.

blocks.text: 11. Large Language Models (LLMs): Module Complete

items: Beam search tracks several partial sequences, beams, in parallel rather than committing to one.
Unlike greedy decoding, an early good-looking choice does not permanently lock in the final sequence.
At each step, beams expand with several possible next words, then only the top-scoring beams survive.
Each beam's score is the sum of log probabilities across its tokens, avoiding extremely tiny numbers.
A wider beam explores more candidates and often finds better results, at proportionally higher compute cost.
Beam search searches deterministically for the single most likely sequence, unlike random sampling.
It suits tasks needing one single best, reliable answer; sampling suits varied, creative generation.
